newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN OLOS SEEN CLOSING IN ON BUNDS ON WAY DOWN.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN OLOS SEEN CLOSING IN ON BUNDS ON WAY DOWN.

text.p: The yield spread of Belgian linear state bonds (OLO) over Bunds could tighten on Friday if late slippage by Bunds on Thursday continued, dealers said.

"It's always the same story when trade is thin and there's no follow-through buying and selling: we lag. When the Bund went up this morning the spread touched 15 basis points, now with the Bund going down it's 13," one trader said. "It's not excluded we could go to 12 or 10 (on Friday) afternoon if this continues."
The benchmark 10-year OLO yielded 5.99 percent at 1510 GMT, up from 5.94 early on Thursday and 5.97 on Wednesday.
The spread over 10-year Bunds was at 13 basis points, down from 14 on Wednesday.

European markets were supported mostly by a set of benign German inflation data, which helped the Bund to resist a weak Wednesday performance in U.S. Treasuries and test the upside. But another weak start in the U.S. late on Thursday afternoon sent European markets into reverse.

One OLO dealer said he doubted the Belgian market would get any support from news late on Thursday that the National Bank of Belgium's leading indicator stopped rising in March, pointing to more pessimistic expectations among economic operators.

"For the moment Belgian investors are watching other countries rather than our own market. We can have good or bad figures here but they are quite neutral. It's France and Germany which are driving the market," he said.

Traders said volume on Thursday remained thin, with business dominated -- as earlier in the week -- by investors taking profits on shorter maturities in favour of longer-dated paper offering a higher yield.
"There was some domestic extending (of portfolios) by buying the 10-year area, but it was very thin," one trader said.

The new OLO 27 (Jan 2000), launched on Monday, continued to get a mixed reception from end-investors, dealers said. Its yield ended at a little changed 4.04 percent after touching 3.99 percent in early trade.
"I see only professional demand for this bond," one trader said, noting it would give holders an option to switch into longer-dated paper from exchange auctions from early 1999.
